content: Monitoring for drug toxicity has become an essential aspect of treatment and prevention programs for pregnant and breastfeeding women. Among the most frequently reported reasons for non-adherence, discontinuation, or substitution of antiretroviral therapy (ART) are toxicities associated with antiretroviral (ARV) drugs. The World Health Organization (WHO) advises countries to adopt a standardized approach to incorporate toxicity monitoring into their national monitoring and evaluation (M&E) systems. This approach includes defining a minimum set of data elements to report the extent of toxicities and their impact on treatment discontinuation. WHO also recommends complementing routine monitoring with active toxicity surveillance through specialized studies and surveys at sentinel sites to address specific concerns. Routine monitoring provides critical data on the incidence and clinical significance of serious ARV toxicities, as well as their effects on patient outcomes and retention in care. This information is vital for guiding strategies to prevent and mitigate drug toxicity, thereby optimizing patient retention and improving treatment effectiveness. For the first time, a specific indicator for toxicity monitoring has been designated for national program monitoring. Disaggregating data by ART regimen, sex, age, pregnancy status, TB/HIV co-infection, and key populations (where data is available) can provide additional insights into populations at higher risk for toxicity due to environmental, behavioral, or co-morbid factors, as well as the concurrent use of other medications. WHO emphasizes strengthening surveillance of key ARV toxicities at sentinel sites when additional data is needed to inform policy and improve treatment outcomes. Active surveillance for specific ARV toxicities can be integrated into existing sentinel cohorts, which already have reliable systems for capturing clinical and toxicity data. Focusing on specific drugs or key toxicities can enhance the accuracy of assessments. Special attention is required for monitoring ARV toxicity during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Routine monitoring of adverse birth outcomes, such as stillbirths, preterm births, low birth weight, and congenital anomalies, can be integrated into national M&E systems. WHO recommends routine monitoring of ARV toxicity during pregnancy and breastfeeding, focusing on three key areas: maternal adverse outcomes (e.g., treatment-limiting toxicities), adverse birth outcomes (e.g., stillbirths, preterm births, and congenital anomalies), and adverse infant and child outcomes (e.g. If adverse birth outcomes are reported at rates higher than expected, formal assessments are warranted to guide national policies on ARV use during pregnancy. The emergence of HIV drug resistance (HIVDR) is a growing global concern, threatening the effectiveness of ART programs and sustained reductions in HIV-related morbidity and mortality. WHO recommends integrating HIVDR prevention and assessment into all national HIV programs. Routine monitoring of early warning indicators (EWIs) and periodic HIVDR surveys in specific populations are essential to inform ART regimen selection and viral load monitoring frequency. WHO's HIVDR strategy promotes the use of EWIs to identify conditions that favor virological failure and the emergence of population-level HIVDR. WHO recommends scaling up VL monitoring to assess the proportion of people living with HIV who achieve virological suppression. This metric is essential for evaluating treatment success, reducing HIV transmission, and guiding quality improvement efforts. In well-performing ART programs, the majority of patients on treatment are expected to achieve suppressed VLs, effectively lowering the risk of HIV transmission. Monitoring VL suppression at specific time points, such as 6, 12, and 48 months after ART initiation, provides valuable insights into long-term treatment outcomes and the quality of care. Population-level VL data can also inform HIV transmission dynamics and the overall effectiveness of ART programs. WHO advises countries to routinely review available VL data to monitor suppression rates and address gaps in testing coverage. Mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HIV accounts for over 90% of pediatric HIV infections. Without any antiretroviral intervention, the risk of MTCT is approximately 30–35%. Transmission can occur during pregnancy, labor, delivery, and breastfeeding. The use of highly effective interventions is critical to reducing this risk and improving outcomes for both mothers and infants.
